title: Squares, Cubes and Roots (Positive and Negative)
kicker: Cambridge Lower Secondary · Mathematics 0862 · Stage 8 · Number
summary: Square and cube positive and negative numbers, find both square roots of a number and the single cube root, estimate roots, and use powers and roots in longer calculations.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Recognise the squares of positive and negative numbers, for example (−6)^{2} = 36, and the square roots that go with them, for example the square roots of 36 are 6 and −6 (8Ni.06)
Recognise positive and negative cube numbers, for example (−4)^{3} = −64, and their cube roots, for example ∛(−64) = −4 (8Ni.07)

blocks.text: In Stage 7 you learned the square numbers and the cube numbers made from positive whole numbers. In Stage 8 you go further: you square and cube **negative** numbers, you learn that a positive number has **two** square roots, and you see why a cube root can be negative. This page also shows you how to estimate roots that are not whole numbers, and how to use roots and powers inside longer calculations.
Key words

items: square (verb)
يربّع — multiply a number by itself: 5^{2} = 5 × 5 = 25
square number
عدد مربع — the answer when a whole number is squared: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 …
square root (√)
الجذر التربيعي — the number that was squared: the square roots of 25 are 5 and −5; √25 = 5
cube (verb)
يكعّب — multiply a number by itself three times: 4^{3} = 4 × 4 × 4 = 64
cube number
عدد مكعب — the answer when a whole number is cubed: 1, 8, 27, 64 … and −1, −8, −27 …
cube root (∛)
الجذر التكعيبي — the number that was cubed: ∛64 = 4 and ∛(−64) = −4
index / power
الأس — the small raised number: in 7^{3} the index 3 tells you how many 7s are multiplied
integer
عدد صحيح — a whole number: positive, negative or zero
inverse
العملية العكسية — the operation that undoes another: square root undoes squaring

blocks.text: 1. Squares and cubes: the pictures behind the words

A **square number** is the area of a square whose sides are a whole number long. A **cube number** is the volume of a cube made from small unit cubes. That is why we say "squared" for the power 2 and "cubed" for the power 3.

blocks.text: You should **know these by heart** for the non-calculator paper. Learn the squares up to 15^{2} and the cubes of 1 to 5 and 10.
2. Squaring negative numbers
Squaring means multiplying a number by **itself**. When the number is negative, you multiply two negatives, and negative × negative = positive.
**Rule:** the square of any number that is not zero is **positive**. So 6^{2} and (−6)^{2} give the same answer, 36.

blocks.title: Brackets change everything: (−5)^{2} is not −5^{2}
items: (−5)^{2} means (−5) × (−5) = **25**. The bracket says: square the whole of −5.
−5^{2} means −(5^{2}) = −(5 × 5) = **−25**. Indices come before the minus sign in the order of operations, so only the 5 is squared.
On a calculator, type the bracket: ( (−) 5 ) x² gives 25. Without the bracket many calculators give −25.

blocks.text: 3. Square roots: two answers, one symbol
Finding a **square root** is the **inverse** (opposite) of squaring. Ask: "Which number, multiplied by itself, gives this?" For 9 there are **two** answers, because 3 × 3 = 9 **and** (−3) × (−3) = 9.

blocks.text: The sign ± is read "plus or minus". So ±7 means "7 or −7". Remember: **a negative number has no square root** in the numbers you use at Stage 8, because every square is positive or zero.
**Square roots of bigger squares.** Use what you know: 30^{2} = 900, so √900 = 30. 400 = 20^{2}, so the square roots of 400 are ±20. For 1600, think 40 × 40 = 1600, so √1600 = 40.
4. Cubing negative numbers and cube roots
Cubing multiplies **three** copies of the number. With a negative number, the first two negatives make a positive, and the third makes it negative again:
**Rule:** the cube of a positive number is positive; the cube of a negative number is **negative**. Cubing keeps the sign.

blocks.text: Because cubing keeps the sign, every number has exactly **one** cube root, and you **can** find the cube root of a negative number:

blocks.title: افتكر القاعدة دي
items: المربع دايماً موجب: (−٣)^{2} = ٩ زي ٣^{2} = ٩. علشان كده العدد الموجب له جذرين تربيعيين: ٣ و −٣. لكن علامة √ لوحدها معناها الجذر الموجب بس: √٩ = ٣.
المكعب بيحافظ على الإشارة: (−٢)^{3} = −٨. علشان كده الجذر التكعيبي واحد بس وليه نفس الإشارة: ∛(−٨) = −٢.
خلي بالك من القوس: (−٥)^{2} = ٢٥ لكن −٥^{2} = −٢٥.

blocks.text: 5. Estimating roots that are not whole numbers
√40 is not a whole number, because 40 is not a square number. You can still say **which two whole numbers it lies between**:

items: Find the square numbers either side of 40: 36 and 49.
Take their square roots: √36 = 6 and √49 = 7.
40 is 4 away from 36 but 9 away from 49, so √40 is **nearer to 6**. (A calculator gives 6.324…)

blocks.text: Cube roots work the same way with cube numbers: 27 < 50 < 64, so 3 < ∛50 < 4. For a negative number, −64 < −50 < −27, so −4 < ∛(−50) < −3.
6. Powers and roots inside longer calculations
Powers and roots come **after brackets** and **before** ×, ÷, + and −. A root sign that covers a whole expression acts like a bracket: work out everything under it first.
**Substituting negative numbers.** When a letter stands for a negative number, put it in a bracket before you square or cube: if x = −3, then x^{2} = (−3)^{2} = 9 and x^{3} = (−3)^{3} = −27.
Worked examples
**Worked example 1** — Work out (a) (−7)^{2} (b) −7^{2} (c) (−1)^{3} [3 marks]

items: (a) (−7) × (−7) = **49** (negative × negative = positive).
(b) Square first, then apply the minus: −(7 × 7) = **−49**.

blocks.text: **Common mistake:** giving 49 for part (b). Without a bracket, only the 7 is squared.
**Worked example 2** — (a) Write down the value of √121. (b) Write down all the solutions of x^{2} = 121. [2 marks]

items: (a) 11 × 11 = 121, and √ means the positive root: **√121 = 11**.
(b) Both 11 and −11 square to 121: **x = 11 or x = −11** (x = ±11).

blocks.text: **Common mistake:** giving only 11 in part (b). "Solutions" or "all the values" means give both.
**Worked example 3** — Work out ∛(−216). [1 mark]

Find the cube root of 216 first by trying cubes: 5^{3} = 125 (too small), 6^{3} = 6 × 6 × 6 = 36 × 6 = 216 ✓. The number is negative, and cubing keeps the sign, so ∛(−216) = **−6**. Check: (−6) × (−6) × (−6) = 36 × (−6) = −216 ✓.
**Worked example 4** — Ring the two whole numbers that √90 lies between: 8 and 9 / 9 and 10 / 10 and 11 / 44 and 46 [1 mark]

Square numbers near 90: 81 = 9^{2} and 100 = 10^{2}. 81 < 90 < 100, so **9 < √90 < 10**: ring "9 and 10". **Common mistake:** halving 90 and choosing "44 and 46" — a square root is not half of the number.
**Worked example 5** — Sami says, "√(25 − 16) is the same as √25 − √16." Is he correct? Show how you decide. [2 marks]

items: √(25 − 16) = √9 = 3 (work under the root first).
3 ≠ 1, so **Sami is not correct**. (1 mark for each value, or for one value and a correct conclusion.)

blocks.text: **Worked example 6** — Find the value of 2a^{2} − a^{3} when a = −3. [2 marks]
**Common mistake:** writing −3^{2} = −9 instead of (−3)^{2} = 9, or forgetting that subtracting −27 means adding 27.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Thinking 5^{2} = 10 or 4^{3} = 12. Squaring is 5 × 5, not 5 × 2; cubing is 4 × 4 × 4, not 4 × 3.
Writing −6^{2} = 36. Without a bracket only the 6 is squared: −6^{2} = −36, but (−6)^{2} = 36.
Giving only the positive answer when the question asks for "the square roots" or "all solutions" of x^{2} = 64. Give ±8.
Writing √25 = ±5. The symbol √ on its own means the positive root: √25 = 5.
Saying ∛(−8) is impossible. It is −2, because (−2)^{3} = −8. It is the **square** root of a negative number that does not exist.
Saying (−2)^{3} = 8. Count the negatives: three negatives multiply to a negative.
Splitting a root over + or −: √(9 + 16) is 5, not 3 + 4 = 7.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: Short "work out" questions with negative numbers, e.g. (−4)^{2} or ∛(−125), usually worth 1 mark each. These are on the non-calculator paper, so know the squares and cubes in the tables above.
"Draw a ring around" the correct value or the two numbers a root lies between.
"Tick (✓) Correct or Not correct" for a student's statement, then explain. Give a calculation as your reason, e.g. "(−3)^{2} = 9, not −9".
"Write down all the solutions" or "Find both values of x" — this is the signal to give the positive **and** negative square root.
Substitution: "Find the value of … when x = −2." Write the bracket (−2) every time.
Investigation-style (Thinking and Working Mathematically): "Give an example to show that … is false" — one correct counter-example is enough, e.g. 0.5^{2} = 0.25 is smaller than 0.5.

blocks.title: إزاي تجاوب في الامتحان
items: لو السؤال قال «كل الحلول» أو «الجذرين التربيعيين» اكتب الإجابة الموجبة والسالبة: ±٨.
لو لقيت √ لوحدها اكتب الجذر الموجب بس.
عوّض بالعدد السالب جوه قوس دايماً: (−٢)^{2} مش −٢^{2}.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Squares, cubes and roots — practice
blocks.intro: 14 questions, from easy to Checkpoint-hard. No calculator. Type negative numbers with a minus sign, e.g. -5. For the two explain questions, mark yourself with the mark scheme.

questions.e: (−6) × (−6) = 36. Negative × negative = positive. −36 is −6^{2} (no bracket); ±12 comes from 6 × 2.

questions.q: Which of these is **not** a cube number?
questions.e: −8 = (−2)^{3}, 1 = 1^{3}, 27 = 3^{3}. There is no integer that cubes to −9 (between (−2)^{3} = −8 and (−3)^{3} = −27), so −9 is not a cube number.
13 × 13 = 169. The symbol √ means the positive square root, so √169 = 13.
8 × 8 = 64 and (−8) × (−8) = 64, so the square roots of 64 are 8 and −8 (±8).

questions.q: (a) Work out the length of one side of the square.
questions.e: Area of a square = side × side, so side = √81 = 9 cm. (A length cannot be negative, so we use only the positive root.)

questions.q: (b) Work out the length of one edge of the cube.
questions.e: Volume of a cube = edge × edge × edge, so edge = ∛64 = 4 cm, because 4 × 4 × 4 = 64.

questions.q: Draw a ring around the two whole numbers that √70 lies between.
Find the value of x^{3} − x^{2} when x = −2.
questions.e: (−2)^{3} − (−2)^{2} = −8 − 4 = −12. 1 mark for −8 or 4 seen (the two powers worked out correctly).

questions.q: Hassan says, "There are two numbers that cube to give −8. They are 2 and −2." Tick Correct or Not correct, and explain your answer.
questions.ms: 1 mark: Not correct, with a reason, e.g. 2^{3} = 8 (not −8) so only −2 works; or (−2)^{3} = −8 but 2^{3} = 8; or a cube root has only one value with the same sign. Do not accept "Not correct" with no reason or a wrong reason.
questions.e: Not correct. 2 × 2 × 2 = 8, which is positive. Only (−2) × (−2) × (−2) = −8. Cubing keeps the sign, so −8 has only one cube root: −2. Hassan is mixing this up with square roots, where 4 has two roots, 2 and −2.

questions.q: Mona says, "When you square a number, the answer is always bigger than the number you started with." Give an example to show that Mona is wrong.
questions.ms: 1 mark: any correct counter-example with its square shown, e.g. 1^{2} = 1 (not bigger); 0^{2} = 0; 0.5^{2} = 0.25; (1/2)^{2} = 1/4. Any number from 0 to 1 inclusive works. Do not accept negative numbers (their squares are bigger) or an example with no value shown.
questions.e: One counter-example is enough. For example 0.5^{2} = 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25, and 0.25 is smaller than 0.5. Also 1^{2} = 1, which is not bigger than 1. (A negative number does not work: (−3)^{2} = 9 is bigger than −3.)

blocks.title: Remember
items: Squaring a non-zero number always gives a positive answer: (−6)^{2} = 6^{2} = 36.
A positive number has two square roots (±); √ on its own means the positive one. Negative numbers have no square root.
Cubing keeps the sign: (−4)^{3} = −64, so ∛(−64) = −4. Every number has exactly one cube root.
Brackets matter: (−5)^{2} = 25 but −5^{2} = −25. Put negative numbers in brackets when you substitute.
To estimate a root, find the square (or cube) numbers on either side: 36 < 40 < 49 so 6 < √40 < 7.
